newsitem.title: FRANCE: French aerospace head urges govt to cut wage costs.
newsitem.headline: French aerospace head urges govt to cut wage costs.

text.p: The head of the French aerospace industry association urged the new Socialist-led government on Saturday to help companies confront intense global competition by cutting their labour costs.

Serge Dassault, chairman of the Groupement des Industries Francaise Aeronautiques et Spatiales (GIFAS), said in a speech at the Paris air show that despite productivity gains, French companies were hampered by high costs due to heavy employer payroll contributions.

French and European firms are looking to every means to sharpen their competitive edge as big U.S. groups such as Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp, and Raytheon Co and Hughes Electronics Corp, merge to form still more powerful combinations.
"Today, for a net salary of 10,000 francs a month, the firm has to pay 30,000 francs, or three times more," Dassault said.
"Confronted with American and European competitors, this structural competitive disadvantage heavily penalises the whole of the French high technology industry, which will tend to relocate," he said.
High labour costs acted as a brake on hirings, favoured unemployment and blocked pay increases, he said.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has made employment a priority for the three-week-old administration, promising to create 700,000 new youth jobs, shared equally between the public and private sector. The government wants to boost purchasing power and stimulate demand.
France suffers from a record unemployment rate of 12.8 percent. The government has to meet tough budgetary targets next year in order to join a single European currency by 1999.

Dassault, who is chairman of combat plane maker Dassault Aviation, said the aerospace industry employed 96,000 directly, with a further 80,000 indirectly working as subcontractors in 4,000 small and medium-sized firms.

The sector had a total turnover of 108 billion francs in 1996, showing a seven percent increase on the previous year, and contributes a net 30 billion francs a year to public finances, he said. Some 65 percent of that turnover came from exports.

Dassault called on the government to support programmes already being launched, including the Dassault Rafale fighter-bomber, the Helios II military spy satellite, and the Tiger and NH90 military helicopters.

The government should create conditions favourable for launching projects such as Airbus Industrie's A340-600 passenger jet, the AirJet 70 regional plane from the AI(R) consortium, the Future Large Aircraft (FLA) military transporter, as well the Trimilsatcomm military satellites.
Dassault also urged the government to increase the amount of launch aid available for new programmes and to re-inject the 1.5 billion francs repaid each year by the industry to government.
The week-long air show closes on Sunday.
